passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday.

Jagdish has been quiet this week. At lunch he sits on the steps near the library with his tiffin, watching the chess club by the window. Until last month, he and Nitin were always together at recess, building forts out of benches.

Nitin joined the chess club three weeks ago. He's there every lunch now with four new friends. I asked him about Jagdish; he looked puzzled and said, "We're still friends. I'm just busy."

Today Jagdish asked me, very softly, "Ma'am, did I do something bad to Nitin?" His eyes were wet.

I told him I didn't think so, that sometimes people get busy with new things. I suggested he ask Nitin to play on Saturday. I'll also mention the chess club to Jagdish; he might like it.

qa.q: What club did Nitin join?
qa.a: Nitin joined the chess club.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he asked if he'd done something bad?
qa.a: He felt hurt and confused, a dull ache of being left behind, and assumed the drift was his fault.

qa.q: How can the teacher help Jagdish now?
qa.a: By gently explaining the drift isn't rejection, encouraging a Saturday invite to Nitin, and helping Jagdish find his own new activity.

qa.q: How does Nitin see the change in their friendship?
qa.a: Nitin doesn't see it as a change at all; he feels they are still friends and is simply busy with new company.

grounding: A teacher sees a child left behind by a busy friend assume he did something wrong, when the drift comes only from new activities.

passage:
In the village of Kumbhalgarh, Pranav's Papa found him sitting by the well, throwing pebbles.

"Elizabeth doesn't play with me anymore," Pranav said. "She plays with the big kids at the church now."

Papa sat down beside him. "Do you miss her?"

Pranav nodded.

"Maybe you can just say hello tomorrow. And ask her to play marbles once. Just once."

"What if she says no?"

"Then she says no, and you'll still have the good days you had. Those were real, beta. Friends sometimes change, like seasons."

The next evening Pranav walked to the church steps. "Elizabeth, want to play marbles?"

She hesitated, then grinned. "One game."

They played two. Then she ran back to the big kids, and Pranav walked home, lighter.

qa.q: Where did Papa find Pranav?
qa.a: Papa found Pranav sitting by the well, throwing pebbles.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: He felt lighter and happier, glad he'd tried even though Elizabeth went back to the big kids.

qa.q: What did Papa do that helped Pranav?
qa.a: He listened, suggested one small invitation, and helped Pranav see that the old friendship was real even if things change.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel when Pranav invites her?
qa.a: Elizabeth may feel a bit surprised and pleased to be remembered, which is why she agreed to a game.

grounding: A parent helps a child say hello and invite an old friend to one game, accepting that friendships change with seasons.

passage:
So, the first month in the Delhi hostel? I'm Yamini, and I said yes to everything. Everything.

Instant noodles at 2 a.m. in Room 14? Yes. Chai walk to the gate at midnight? Yes. Someone's cousin's birthday in Lajpat Nagar? Absolutely yes.

I was so lonely those first nights that any open door felt like a lifeline. And Sudha, from Room 16, she was the same. We'd sit on her floor talking about how much we missed home, her mother's rasam, my brother's awful jokes. By week three we were calling each other "sister."

Looking back, it was real, but it was also fast. We knew each other's childhood fears before we knew each other's middle names. It felt like we'd been friends for years. It had been nineteen days.

qa.q: Which room was Sudha in?
qa.a: Sudha was in Room 16.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling in those first nights at the hostel?
qa.a: Yamini felt lonely and homesick, so every open door and invitation felt like a lifeline.

qa.q: What could Yamini keep in mind as these quick friendships grow?
qa.a: That early closeness can feel stronger than it is yet, so it helps to let trust build over time while enjoying it.

qa.q: How might Sudha have felt about their quick bond?
qa.a: Sudha seemed equally lonely and glad of the company, finding comfort in sharing homesickness.

grounding: A spoken account shows a lonely young adult saying yes to every hostel invitation, with shared homesickness creating quick intimacy.

passage:
Buddy programme note, first-year hostel, week 6. Written by the student mentor coordinator.

Pairing Hansa and Gargi appears to be working. At the start, both mostly talked about classes. In today's check-in, they asked to meet me together.

Gargi said she had told Hansa about her parents' separation, which no one else at college knows. She said she'd watched Hansa's face "to see if she'd pity me or judge me." Hansa didn't do either; she just said, "That sounds lonely," and then told Gargi about her own fear of failing and letting her father down.

Hansa said that after that night, she felt "like I had a person here."

I noticed how carefully each watched the other while telling their story. That seems to be what they were really testing: whether it was safe.

No action needed. Will continue fortnightly check-ins.

qa.q: What did Hansa say after Gargi shared about her parents?
qa.a: Hansa said, "That sounds lonely."

qa.q: What was Gargi afraid of when telling Hansa about the separation?
qa.a: Gargi was afraid Hansa would pity or judge her, so she watched Hansa's face closely.

qa.q: Why did Hansa's response help the friendship deepen?
qa.a: She responded with care and then shared her own fear, which made the disclosure mutual and showed it was safe.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel after that night?
qa.a: Hansa felt she finally had someone at college, a sense of belonging and trust.

grounding: A mentor's note shows two new friends sharing family troubles and fears in turn, each checking whether the other responds with care.

subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]
passage:
"Do they ever do anything alone?" Shreya asked, nodding at the table by the canteen window.

Nitin looked up from his samosa. "Who, my lot?"

"Your lot. Five of you. Breakfast together, library together, you all went to Rishikesh together. I transferred in August and I've never seen one of you without the other four."

Nitin laughed. "It's nice, na? You always have people."

"It looks nice. But when I asked Tanmay to join the photography club, he said, 'The group won't like it.' Like it's a rule."

Nitin paused, samosa halfway. "Nobody said that."

"Nobody has to say it."

He looked at the table, where the others were saving his chair. "Maybe. I did skip the theatre workshop because they'd all be at the movie."

Shreya shrugged. "Just saying. From outside, it's cosy. And a bit tight."

qa.q: When did Shreya transfer?
qa.a: Shreya transferred in August.

qa.q: What might Shreya be feeling as she watches the group?
qa.a: Shreya seems curious and a little wistful, admiring the closeness but uneasy about how tight it looks.

qa.q: What could Nitin try, based on this conversation?
qa.a: He could join the theatre workshop or another activity on his own, and say openly to the group that seeing other friends is okay.

qa.q: How does Nitin see his group at first, and what changes?
qa.a: At first he sees only the comfort of always having people; then he realises he has skipped things to stay with them.

grounding: An outsider notices a close college group doing everything together, comforting but carrying unspoken pressure not to seek other friends.

passage:
The call dropped for the third time. Ganga was on the rooftop of her Bengaluru PG, the only place with signal, and it had started to drizzle.

Aparna's face froze on the screen, mid-sentence. Then: "Network weak."

It had been like this since college ended. Ganga had the placement in Bengaluru. Aparna had stayed in Jaipur and was working evenings at her uncle's shop because her family needed the money. Their third friend, Sonal, now only posted pictures with her boyfriend.

Once, they'd talked every night. Now it was hearts on each other's posts. Ganga had missed Aparna's birthday call by a whole day. Aparna hadn't asked about Ganga's new job.

Ganga typed, "Sorry, net's bad. Talk soon?" and felt guilty even as she sent it. She knew Aparna probably felt guilty too. Neither of them would say "soon" meant nothing.

qa.q: Where was Ganga's PG?
qa.a: Ganga's PG was in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she sent 'Talk soon?'
qa.a: She felt guilty, knowing the friendship was slipping and suspecting 'soon' might not happen.

qa.q: What small step could keep this friendship alive despite the distance?
qa.a: Ganga could suggest a fixed short call once a week at a time that fits Aparna's evening shifts, so they don't rely on chance.

qa.q: How might Aparna be experiencing the drift?
qa.a: Aparna is busy and under pressure at the shop, and likely also feels guilty for not asking about Ganga's job.

grounding: With poor signal and different lives, friends drift as calls turn into likes, and each feels guilty for not calling.

passage:
You asked why I looked sad scrolling through my phone. Okay. I'm Mahima, and I just realised something stupid.

Vinita and I were inseparable in first year. Every exam, every heartbreak, every terrible mess dinner. Then she moved to the other campus for her specialisation. We said we'd meet every Sunday.

I scrolled up just now. Our last real conversation was in March. It's October. Since then? Birthday wishes. A few hearts. One "we should catch up!!" that neither of us followed up.

Nothing happened. No fight. Nobody did anything wrong. That's what makes it strange. If we'd fought, I'd know what to be sad about.

But I am sad. It feels like losing someone, and I don't think I'm allowed to call it that, because she's still right there on my phone.

qa.q: When was Mahima's last real conversation with Vinita?
qa.a: It was in March.

qa.q: What is Mahima feeling after scrolling through the chat?
qa.a: Mahima feels a quiet sadness and grief, like a loss, but unsure it's allowed since there was no fight.

qa.q: What could Mahima do with this feeling?
qa.a: Mahima could let the sadness be real, and if the friendship still matters, send Vinita a specific message suggesting a time to talk.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel if she noticed the same gap?
qa.a: Vinita might feel the same quiet sadness and guilt, perhaps waiting for Mahima to reach out first.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone realising months have passed without a real talk and grieving a friendship that faded with no single cause.

passage:
Wednesday: Alka found an old photo of herself and Farida at the college canteen, two cups of chai, Farida laughing at something off-camera. They hadn't really talked in eight months. Alka typed "miss you!!" and deleted it. Too vague.

Friday: She wrote instead: "I was thinking of our Sunday chai at the canteen. Can we talk this weekend? Just half an hour?" She sent it before she could change her mind.

Sunday: Farida called at eleven. They talked for an hour and a half. It wasn't the same as before, but it was good.

Later that evening, Alka looked at her other old group chat, silent since June. She thought about those friends with warmth and a little sadness. She decided not everyone needed a message. Some chapters were just finished, and she was grateful for them.

qa.q: What did Alka find on Wednesday?
qa.a: She found an old photo of herself and Farida at the college canteen.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling on Sunday evening about the old group chat?
qa.a: She felt warm, a little sad and grateful, accepting that some friendships were simply finished.

qa.q: Why was Alka's Friday message better than 'miss you!!'?
qa.a: It was specific, recalled a shared ritual and asked for a clear, small plan, which made it easy for Farida to say yes.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt receiving Alka's message?
qa.a: Farida was probably touched and glad to be remembered, which is why she called on Sunday.

grounding: Over several days a young adult sends a specific message to revive one friendship and lets another go with gratitude.

subtype: Stage 1: Trust and a shared secret [Receiver]
passage:
The school bus was stuck in the rain on the Sion flyover, and nobody was going anywhere for an hour.

Kashish sat at the back with Shankar, her best friend since Class 6. The windows fogged. Everyone else was asleep or on their phones.

"Can I tell you two things?" she said, very quietly. "Promise you won't laugh."

"Promise."

"I like Aman. From the debate team."

Shankar's eyes widened, but he didn't laugh. "Okay. That's big."

"And... Papa lost his job in June. We might have to move to a smaller flat. I haven't told anyone."

Shankar was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "Thank you for telling me. I won't tell anyone. Either thing."

Kashish leaned her head against the fogged window. Her chest felt loose for the first time in weeks, like she'd put down a heavy bag.

qa.q: Where was the school bus stuck?
qa.a: It was stuck in the rain on the Sion flyover.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling after telling Shankar?
qa.a: She felt lighter and relieved, as if she'd put down a heavy bag, because Shankar received her secrets with care.

qa.q: What could Kashish do if the worries about home keep weighing on her?
qa.a: She could also talk to a trusted adult, like a parent or school counsellor, while keeping Shankar as a support.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel being trusted with these secrets?
qa.a: Shankar likely feels honoured and protective, promising to keep both things private.

grounding: Stuck in traffic, a teen tells her closest friend about her crush and family money worries, feeling lighter for being known.

subtopic: Friendship betrayal to reconciliation or ending
passage:
Madhuri had exactly ten minutes before the bell, and the new group had finally let her sit with them on the steps.

Varun, who everyone wanted to impress, was telling a story about a teacher. Then someone said, "Madhuri, you're friends with Tanu, right? She's so quiet. Does she even like anyone?"

Everyone looked at her. For the first time, they were interested.

"Actually," Madhuri said, before she could stop herself, "she has a huge crush on Imtiaz. Like, huge."

The group burst into delighted noises. Varun grinned at her.

It's not a big deal, Madhuri told herself. Everyone has crushes. The bell rang, and she walked to class feeling like she belonged.

It was only that night, when she saw Tanu's message, "Why is everyone teasing me about Imtiaz??", that the weight of it hit her.

qa.q: How long did Madhuri have before the bell?
qa.a: She had exactly ten minutes before the bell.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she saw Tanu's message that night?
qa.a: She suddenly felt guilty and heavy, realising she'd betrayed Tanu's trust just to seem interesting.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Madhuri now?
qa.a: She could admit to Tanu that she told the group and apologise without excuses, and ask the group to stop teasing.

qa.q: How might Tanu feel when everyone starts teasing her?
qa.a: Tanu is likely confused, embarrassed and hurt, not yet knowing who revealed her secret.

grounding: Wanting to seem interesting to a new group, a teen lets slip a friend's secret, tells herself it is nothing and only later feels its weight.
